title: US Open tennis: Fritz, Anisimova and Keys in action on day seven – live
text:
The first five points of the breaker go the way of the server … until Zheng nails a forehand winner down the line off Keys’s drop shot! Zheng has a 4-2 lead at the change of ends … Keys takes the next point with a winner into pretty much exactly the same spot as Zheng’s landed … but Zheng still has the advantage and extends that to 5-3 and then 6-3 with two big serves. Zheng has three set points … and Keys hits beyond the baseline! That was a flawless tie-break from the Olympic champion and they’re going to a third. It’s Keys 6-1, 6-7 (3) Zheng.
Keys holds. Zheng holds. It means Keys is serving to stay in the second set at 5-6. There were some really strong quotes from Keys after the first round, when she spoke about how intensely nervous she felt before the match, especially as a home player. It was interesting to hear how the nerves can affect even last year’s Australian Open champion. But there’s no sign of any now, as she holds to 15. So it’s tie-break time.
Fritz, after conceding only two games in the previous round, has dropped two in six games today. Crisis! He leads Cerundolo 4-2.
Keys, Zheng and Anisimova are all wearing very similar turquoise Nike outfits. Which is making things slightly confusing, it has to be said. Almost as confusing as keeping up with the Anisimova v Potapova scoreline, after a fourth successive break. Anisimova eventually snaps the streak with a hold, and she’s 3-2 up in the second set. Can she build on this?
What of Keys v Zheng, you say? Well after a very cagey second set, Zheng strikes in game eight – as Keys clunks an errant forehand and coughs up a double fault from deuce. It leaves Zheng serving to level the match at 5-3 – but a meek second serve gets the treatment it deserves at 30-all and Keys has break point. And the break is retrieved after some more heavy hitting from the American! It’s Keys 6-1, 4-5 Zheng.
Now it’s three consecutive breaks at the start of the second. Anisimova has held serve only twice in the match – and now trails 6-2, 2-1.
Finally Anisimova gets a break against Potapova – though she needed a double fault from the Austrian on break point to do it – and all it does is get her level in the second set, because she was broken in the previous game. So it’s Anisimova 2-6, 1-1 Potapova.
Fritz’s problem this season has been staying fit – but when he’s healthy, he’s a serious contender, shown by his hard-court title in Washington DC last month. He’s also got the experience of going deep in New York, having reached the final two years ago. But he is in a fairly loaded quarter of the draw, which includes Flavio Cobolli and Jakub Mensik.
Fritz, having flown through his previous match for the loss of only two games, for the most emphatic win of his grand slam career, has carried on where he left off, and he already leads Cerundolo, this summer’s Queen’s champion, 3-0.
Anisimova surrenders another break – she’s 0-7 on break points and Potapova 2-4, which is the story of the first set, along with the 19 unforced errors that Anisimova has hit – and Potapova is, unexpectedly, serving for the opener. And Potapova takes it on her fourth set point, 6-2, when Anisimova’s return loops long! Last year’s runner-up has got plenty to tidy up in her game if she’s to turn this match around.
Here’s Tumaini’s report on that match:
In the end, after so much toil and admirable fight, defeat came swiftly for one of the greatest doubles teams to ever share a tennis court. Upon their return to prime time in New York, Venus and Serena Williams fought desperately to overturn the various deficits they found themselves in over three hours inside a thunderous Arthur Ashe Stadium.
They came close. The Williams sisters had clawed their way back into the match after trailing a 1-4 in their final set against Chan Hao-ching and Maya Joint, and they established a 5-0 lead in the third set tie-break. Just as they appeared to be on the verge of victory, they were brushed aside, losing 6-3, 6-7 (6), 7-6 (7) in the first round of the US Open.
This was one of the few times in recent tennis history where a player’s doubles appearance seemed far more important than their singles contributions. While the 44-year-old Serena had opted out of taking a singles wildcard for the US Open after suffering a knee injury during her singles comeback at Wimbledon in July against Joint, the 46-year-old Venus lost in the singles first round here to Sofia Kenin, her 15th consecutive singles loss. No matter, from the moment it became clear that the Williams sisters were aiming to compete alongside each other in doubles again, this was the match that people wanted to see.
Before this summer, when the Williams sisters finally rejoined forces at the Cincinnati Open, losing in a tight first round battle, the last time Venus and Serena had competed together was here in 2022, supposedly Serena’s final tournament. Serena had been extremely impressive in her mixed doubles appearance alongside Carlos Alcaraz this year, who she had even outperformed for a large part of her matches. Here, perhaps under the additional pressure alongside her sister, the four years of rust was still visible on Serena’s game as she struggled badly throughout the match.
A week after cracking 120mph aces on pressure points, Serena had so many troubles with her serve that, by the final set, she had been reduced to simply rolling in her first serve and she similarly struggled to land any returns. Venus, meanwhile, was often the best player on the court, but the pair paid for her failure to put away key volleys deep in the match.
Regardless, the Williams sisters fought desperately for three hours, produced numerous moments of brilliance and nearly defeated the 14th seed team in the draw. They were eventually outplayed by a solid pairing in Joint, a top 30 doubles player, and the former world No 5 and Wimbledon finalist Chan. The Australian-Taiwanese pair were at times overwhelmed by the increasingly intense crowd inside Arthur Ashe Stadium and their indefatigable opponents. But in the decisive moments deep in the final set tie-break they handled business as they should, absorbing the Williams sisters’ first strike while tidying up around the net.
You can read the rest here:
Last night Serena and Venus Williams – with their combined age of 456 - blew a five-point lead in the deciding tie-break as their return to the grand slam doubles stage ended in defeat, 6-3, 6-7 (6), 7-6 (7) against Chan Hao-ching and Maya Joint. Serena must be sick of the sight of Joint – given her singles comeback was also halted by the Australian in the Wimbledon first round this summer – but having come so close to victory in both matches, she may well be encouraged enough to continue. Serena and Venus chose not to do a post-match media conference last night – so it’s not clear what their next plans are.
A big cheer on Grandstand – despite the fact Zheng is facing an American – as she holds at the start of the second set. Anisimova is still a break down, 3-2, against Potapova, while Taylor Fritz – the pick of the American men in the first week - is warming up on Arthur Ashe against Francisco Cerundolo, the 24th seed from Argentina.
And after my talking-up of Zheng’s chances … she’s 5-1 down in 20 minutes. A messy fourth game, including two double faults, surrendered the first break – and the second came when she was broken to love. So Keys, having survived those five match points against her in round two, is making the most of her second life, serving for the set … and the 2017 runner-up closes it out emphatically, to 15. Perhaps all the matches Zheng has played to get to this point are now catching up with her.
Anisimova, one of the purest and most powerful hitters in the women’s game, is pushing hard on Potapova’s serve at 0-40, and despite being dragged back to deuce, she has another three break points … of which she takes absolutely none. And then she’s promptly broken to love. She’ll be kicking herself. She could be 2-1 up with the break but instead finds herself 2-1 down.
So what of their opponents today? Zheng has greater momentum than Keys coming into the third round. The former world No 4 has won five consecutive matches after coming through qualifying – her world ranking is currently No 121 as she works her way back after elbow surgery last year – and the last time she won five on the spin she claimed the Olympic singles title for China in 2024.
Potapova, meanwhile, the 24th seed, is looking to reach the US Open fourth round for the first time. She gained headlines at the end of last year when she announced she’d switched her allegiance from Russia to Austria, having basically hit copy and paste on the statement her former compatriot Daria Kasatkina made when she started representing Australia last year. As our tennis correspondent Tumaini Carayol explains:
To the bemusement of Kasatkina herself, Potapova changed just two words of Kasatkina’s original before publishing the statement as her own: Australia to Austria and Melbourne to Vienna. Potapova was unapologetic about her lack of originality: “I don’t find anything wrong with that because you cannot say it in a better way. And why not? And, yeah, it was perfect words. I loved it. We loved it with my team, with everyone.”
Keys and Anisimova both start with a hold, but while Keys comes through the opening game reasonably comfortably, to 30, Anisimova has to save two break points at 15-40 before edging through from deuce.
“It’s so wide open,” says Martina Navratilova on Sky Sports about the women’s draw, and I’m in total agreement with her – though I’m not sure even if I did disagree that I’d have the gumption to argue with Martina. Sabalenka, Gauff, Rybakina, Andreeva, Swiatek, Pegula, Anisimova … you really could take your pick. And that’s without even mentioning the Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova, the two-time US Open winner Naomi Osaka, the ever-improving Marta Kostyuk and the rising Iva Jovic and Alexandra Eala. I think this year is too soon for Jovic and Eala – especially as the winner of their match later could face Gauff in the last 16 – but the strength and depth at the top of women’s game is seriously impressive.
The sun is out and two Americans, Amanda Anisimova and Madison Keys, will get this Labor Day weekend under way at Flushing Meadows. Anisimova, last year’s finalist at the US Open and Wimbledon, plays the Russian-born Austrian Anastasia Potapova on Louis Armstrong, while Keys, after her great escape in round two, where she saved five match points, faces the 2024 Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen on Grandstand.

Hello and welcome to the US Open 2026 - day seven! I can’t believe we’re nearly at the halfway stage already, with the top takeaways so far (along with the $100 caviar-topped chicken nuggets) being that:
It’s so good to have Carlos Alcaraz back – even though it’s not the same without Jannik Sinner
The end game appears closer for Novak Djokovic - and has already come for Stan Wawrinka and Gael Monfils – while Alex de Minaur is at a career crossroads
Aryna Sabalenka is working her way back into form – though success isn’t the only thing she’s been smelling
Coco Gauff has served notice with her start – while Elena Rybakina, Iga Swiatek and Mirra Andreeva have impressed too (Gauff, Rybakina and Jessica Pegula are still pushing Sabalenka for the world No 1 spot)
Taylor Fritz is arguably the best-placed home hope to end the 23-year wait for an American male singles champion
Naomi Osaka’s tennis hasn’t been as eye-catching as her latest look
Eala-mania has taken over New York
Britain desperately needs Jack Draper and Emma Raducanu back fit
And Alexander Zverev, looking shaky in his first slam as the No 1 seed, has likely turned into a zombie in the city that never sleeps after two 2am, five-set finishes
Zverev is on the night shift again on day seven, scheduled second on Arthur Ashe in the evening session, after Alexandra Eala v Iva Jovic offers us a tantalising glimpse into the future of women’s tennis – but our focus is on the day session, with Fritz, Gauff, Swiatek, Rybakina and Andreeva all in action, along with Amanda Anisimova, Madison Keys, Flavio Cobolli, the rising American Michael Zheng, Australia’s sole survivor Dane Sweeny and the vanquisher of Felix Auger-Aliassime, Karen Khachanov.
Play gets under way: at 11am local time/4pm BST. Don’t go anywhere!
